prompt: Ignoring air resistance, what is the velocity of a projectile at the highest point of its path?

choices.text: Horizontal, equal to u cos θ

choices.why: Only the vertical component is zero at the top. The horizontal component never changes.

choices.text: Vertical, equal to u sin θ
choices.why: The vertical component is zero at the top, and that is what makes it the top.

choices.text: Equal to the launch speed u
choices.why: The vertical component has been lost, so the speed is smaller than u.

hints: Think about the two components separately.
Is there any horizontal force?
solution: At the top, v_y = 0.
vₓ = u cos θ throughout, because there is no horizontal force.
So the velocity is horizontal and equal to u cos θ.
misconceptions: Thinking a projectile momentarily stops at the top.

prompt: Ignoring air resistance, what is the acceleration of a projectile at the highest point of its path?

choices.text: It depends on the launch angle
choices.why: The only force is weight, so the acceleration is g everywhere on the path.

hints: What forces act on the projectile at the top?
solution: The only force is weight, mg, downwards.
So a = g = 9.81 m s⁻² downwards at every point, including the top.
misconceptions: Zero velocity implies zero acceleration.

prompt: Which condition defines simple harmonic motion? (x is displacement from equilibrium, a is acceleration.)

choices.why: Without the minus sign the acceleration points away from equilibrium and the object would fly off instead of oscillating.
The defining condition is about acceleration, not velocity.
In SHM the acceleration changes continuously; it is zero at equilibrium and greatest at the extremes.

hints: The force must always pull back towards the middle.
solution: SHM requires a = −ω²x: acceleration proportional to displacement and directed towards equilibrium.
misconceptions: Forgetting the minus sign: the restoring direction is the essential feature.

prompt: Where is the speed of an object in SHM greatest?

choices.text: At the extremes of the motion
choices.why: The acceleration is greatest at the extremes; the speed is zero there.

choices.text: Halfway between equilibrium and an extreme
choices.why: The speed keeps increasing all the way to equilibrium.
Kinetic energy and potential energy keep swapping, so the speed changes.

hints: Where is all the energy kinetic?
solution: E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) is greatest when x = 0.
So the speed is greatest at equilibrium: v_max = ωx₀.
misconceptions: Confusing where speed is greatest with where acceleration is greatest.

prompt: Which statement about the half-life of a radioactive isotope is correct?

choices.text: It is the same however many nuclei the sample starts with
It gets shorter as the sample decays
choices.why: Each nucleus has the same fixed probability of decaying, so every halving takes the same time.

choices.text: It is half the time it takes for the whole sample to decay
choices.why: A sample never fully decays; N only approaches zero.

choices.text: It increases when the sample is heated
choices.why: Decay is a nuclear process, unaffected by temperature or chemistry.

hints: Does each nucleus 'know' how many others are around it?
solution: The decay constant λ is a property of the isotope.
T½ = ln 2 / λ, so the half-life is fixed, whatever the sample size.
misconceptions: Half-life is half the total lifetime of the sample.

prompt: Why is it impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay?

choices.text: Decay is random: each nucleus has a constant probability of decaying per unit time
Because it depends on the temperature, which keeps changing
choices.why: Decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.

choices.why: Nuclei do not age: the probability per second is the same for every nucleus, however long it has existed.
